questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz))\,k \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+z\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz))\text{ }j+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(-(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+0\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0))\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
